rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and identify the resolution-limiting pairs while encouraging all 10 compounds to elute. The results will guide window trimming and targeted slope and temperature adjustments.
Only one pair limits the score, while all compounds elute comfortably within 10 minutes. Change temperature alone to test whether selectivity can resolve that pair without lengthening the gradient.

The temperature change improved separation in the original crowded cluster but created a different close pair at 60 C. Test 55 C to balance these competing selectivity effects while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.
Injection 3 achieved the maximum CRF and remains the reference method. Shorten the gradient by two minutes to test whether full resolution can be preserved with faster elution.

The steeper 10-minute gradient compromised resolution, so return to 12 minutes and modestly raise the starting organic fraction. This tests a shorter elution time with a slightly shallower slope, while retaining injection 3 as the maximum-score reference.

Slightly reduce gradient steepness to recover the limiting pair’s resolution at the higher starting organic fraction. This may preserve the maximum CRF while eluting the final peak slightly earlier than injection 3.

Test a cooler selectivity regime with the faster gradient: the temperature-dependent elution-order change suggests cooling may also separate the original limiting pair. This explores a different route to full resolution rather than further slowing the 55 C method.

Injection 3 already achieves the maximum CRF. Test a substantially steeper gradient at 60 C to see whether the temperature-sensitive close pair separates after an elution-order reversal, enabling a much faster fully resolved method.

Test a higher starting organic fraction at 60 C to shift selectivity around the close middle peaks while maintaining a moderate gradient slope. This explores a faster alternative; injection 3 remains the established maximum-score method.

Return to the successful 55 C selectivity and use a narrower, shallower gradient to recover middle-pair resolution at a higher starting organic fraction. Starting at 0.15 should also retain the early peaks better than injection 9.

Injection 6 was nearly fully resolved; reducing its endpoint to 0.85 should improve the slope-sensitive limiting pair while keeping the final peak below 10 minutes. This tests for a maximum-score method with more resolution margin than injection 3.

Preserve injection 3’s successful starting composition, temperature, and gradient slope while removing the unused high-organic portion. All peaks should elute before the gradient ends, retaining CRF 1.000 with a shorter programmed gradient.

Explore a faster alternative to the established maximum-score method. Relative to injection 9, lower the starting organic fraction to improve early-peak retention and steepen the gradient to test separation on the reversed-order side of the temperature-sensitive middle pair.

Prioritize resolution margin now that CRF 1.000 is established. A shallower version of injection 10 should improve its limiting middle pair while retaining adequate early-peak separation and likely keeping the final peak below 10 minutes.

Several methods already achieve the maximum CRF, so test the unexplored low-temperature extreme for a faster fully resolved alternative. Cooling may separate the crowded cluster through selectivity changes, while the shorter gradient limits retention time.

Use a gradient slope between injections 6 and 11, targeting full resolution with earlier final elution than injection 11. The limiting pair is expected to reach approximately R 1.55 while the other close pair remains above 1.5.

Test whether a shallower gradient resolves the crowded cluster seen at 35 C, separating slope effects from temperature effects by comparison with injection 7. The final peak should remain below 10 minutes, leaving a route to another maximum-score selectivity regime.

Slightly flatten injection 16’s gradient to increase the limiting pair’s resolution while keeping the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes. This targets greater separation margin at the already achieved maximum CRF.

Slightly flatten injection 14’s gradient to improve its limiting pair while testing whether the final peak still elutes within 10 minutes. This targets a larger minimum-resolution margin at CRF 1.000; injection 3 remains the faster maximum-score reference.

Test whether cooling injection 9 improves early-peak retention and separates its crowded middle group through temperature-dependent selectivity. This explores a substantially faster alternative while retaining the established CRF 1.000 methods as references.

Flatten injection 20’s gradient to test whether both remaining close pairs gain sufficient resolution while preserving its adequate early-peak separation. The substantial time margin provides room to improve separation without incurring a time penalty.

Use a slope slightly steeper than injection 14 to test faster elution while retaining its improved resolution margin. The limiting pair should remain above R 1.5, targeting another maximum-score method with the last peak near 9 minutes.

Preserve the starting composition, temperature, and 0.075-per-minute slope of the fastest demonstrated maximum-score method. This intermediate endpoint should reproduce full resolution and a 7.60-minute last peak while providing more high-organic hold strength than injection 12.

Test a slope between injections 14 and 19 to balance their two limiting pairs, targeting a minimum resolution near 1.7. All peaks should remain within the gradient and elute before 10 minutes, preserving the maximum CRF with greater separation margin than injection 3.

Use a slope between injections 24 and 19 to balance the two limiting pairs, targeting a minimum resolution near 1.69 with the last peak below 10 minutes. The theoretical maximum CRF is already achieved; this final test seeks additional separation margin.
